titulo: Wilbur and Orville Wright: The First Airplane

fuente.licencia: Dominio público (VOA, gobierno de EE. UU.)
fuente.nota: Text shortened by removing paragraphs; the sentences are unchanged.

parrafos: Wilbur and Orville Wright are the American inventors who made a small engine-powered flying machine. They proved that flight without the aid of gas-filled balloons was possible.

As they grew up, the Wright brothers experimented with mechanical things. Later, the Wright brothers began to design their own flying machine. They used ideas they had developed from earlier experiments with a toy helicopter, kites, the printing machine and bicycles.

Soon, they needed a place to test their ideas about flight. The best place with the best wind conditions seemed to be a piece of sandy land in North Carolina along the coast of the Atlantic Ocean. It was called Kill Devil Hill, near the town of Kitty Hawk.
By the autumn of 1903, Wilbur and Orville had designed and built an airplane powered by a gasoline engine. The plane had wings 12 meters across. It weighed about 340 kilograms, including the pilot.

On December 17th, 1903, they made the world's first flight in a machine that was heavier than air and powered by an engine. Orville flew the plane 36 meters. He was in the air for 12 seconds. The two brothers made three more flights that day.

It was almost five years before the Wright brothers became famous. In 1908, Wilbur went to France. He gave demonstration flights at heights of 90 meters. A French company agreed to begin making the Wright brothers' flying machine.

Orville made successful flights in the United States at the time Wilbur was in France. The United States War Department agreed to buy a Wright brothers' plane. Wilbur and Orville suddenly became world heroes. But the brothers were not seeking fame. They returned to Dayton where they continued to improve their airplanes. They taught many others how to fly.

Today, the Wright brothers' first airplane is in the Air and Space Museum in Washington, D.C. Visitors to the museum can look at the Wright brothers' small plane. Then they can walk to another area and see space vehicles and a rock collected from the moon. The world has changed a lot since Wilbur and Orville Wright began the modern age of flight over one hundred years ago.
titulo_es: Wilbur and Orville Wright: the first aeroplane
resumen_es: A short biography of the Wright brothers, who in 1903, in North Carolina, made the first flight of an engine-powered, heavier-than-air machine, and of how they became famous years later.
nivel_motivo: The sentences are short and the chronological narrative is very clear; only a few technical words (gasoline engine, kites) raise the lexical index, so the text fits B1 better.

ideas_clave.idea: The Wright brothers were American inventors who showed that engine-powered flight was possible without gas balloons.
Their interest in machines and earlier experiments with toys, kites and bicycles inspired their own aircraft, which they tested on a windy, sandy spot near Kitty Hawk, North Carolina.
On 17 December 1903 their gasoline-powered plane made the first engine-driven flight of a heavier-than-air machine, covering 36 metres in 12 seconds.

Fame came only in 1908, after successful demonstrations in France and the United States led to commercial and military orders, yet the brothers went back to Dayton to keep improving their planes and teaching others to fly.
Their first plane is now displayed in Washington next to space vehicles, a reminder of how much the world has changed since they opened the age of flight.

resumen_modelo: The text recounts the achievement of Wilbur and Orville Wright, the American inventors who proved that powered flight did not require balloons. Drawing on earlier experiments with kites and bicycles, they designed an aircraft and tested it near Kitty Hawk, North Carolina, where the wind conditions were ideal. On 17 December 1903, Orville made the first engine-powered flight in a heavier-than-air machine. However, fame only arrived in 1908, following public demonstrations in France and the United States. Their original plane is now exhibited in Washington, a symbol of the modern era of aviation they inaugurated.
